title: Deterministic Fragments Transport — PRD notes
content:
Purpose
This doc captures a lightweight PRD and implementation notes for a deterministic fragment-based transport for incremental response delivery from the Hosted API. The goal is an SDK-friendly protocol that improves resumability, deterministic reassembly on clients, safe tool-calls (structured output envelopes), and clear telemetry for per-fragment cost/latency accounting. This is a working sketch — design trade-offs and API surface are intentionally explored at the client and server boundary.

Context and motivation
- Current partial/streaming work focuses on progressive text frames and ad-hoc JSON chunks. Clients repeatedly handle reordering, partial JSON, and complex tool-call handoffs.
- We want to support: resumable sessions after transient network failures, deterministic patch/merge semantics for structured output (tables, JSON actions), replay-safe tool invocations (idempotent tool-call envelopes), and SDK ergonomics for mobile and constrained clients.
- Business: reduce support incidents from inconsistent partial responses, enable offline resume for mobile apps, and give product teams a clearer billing/latency slice per fragment.

Goals (what success looks like)
- Deterministic reassembly: client can assemble fragments into a stable final output without needing custom heuristics.
- Resume and idempotency: after a disconnect, client can resume at the exact fragment index and avoid duplicate tool invocations.
- Structured tool-calls: tool invocation frames include a guaranteed idempotency token and a simple status lifecycle (requested, accepted, executed, failed).
- SDK ergonomics: high-level client APIs for incremental consumption (onFragment), delta-apply, and backpressure hints; minimal surface area for common SDK languages (JS, Python, mobile).
- Observability: per-fragment metrics (tokens, compute, latency, error) surfaced in Console for debugging and billing reconciliation.

Non-goals
- Not intended to replace full state syncing protocols (CRDTs) — we aim for deterministic linear fragments that represent a single server-side generation pipeline.
- Not an attempt to standardize all tool-call semantics across customers; we provide a minimal envelope and lifetime model.

High-level design
1) Fragment primitives
- Each response is a sequence of numbered fragments. Fragments are immutable, ordered, and have monotonic integer sequence ids (frag_seq).
- Transport carries the fragment payload and a small header: {frag_seq, session_id, resume_token, partial_schema_path?}.
- Payload types: TEXT, PARTIAL_JSON, ACTION_CALL, META (progress/markers).

2) Deterministic merging rules (clients)
- Clients append fragments in frag_seq order. If frag_seq gaps are detected, client requests resume from the last contiguous frag_seq + 1 using resume_token.
- PARTIAL_JSON fragments are guaranteed to be syntactically self-contained if annotated with partial_schema_path; otherwise client applies them as string concat with whitespace normalization.
- ACTION_CALL fragments encode a structured tool call (see section) — client must not re-run tool-side effects unless a tool-call is explicitly re-acknowledged by server with a tool_execution_id and a final state.

3) Resume semantics and tokens
- resume_token is an opaque server-provided token that represents server-side generation state and the last frag_seq committed for that client route. Client stores it locally whenever the last-frag is acknowledged.
- On reconnect, client calls /resume with session_id and resume_token. Server validates token and streams missing fragments from last acknowledged seq. If token expired, server responds with a session-reset flag and a best-effort rerun (client should alert user if deterministic reassembly is impossible).

4) Tool-call envelope and idempotency
- ACTION_CALL fragment fields (stringified for transport): action_id (client-generated UUID or server-assigned), action_spec (structured JSON describing call), client_asserted_inputs (optional), expectations (sync/async), idempotency_key.
- Server returns ACTION_ACK fragment with tool_execution_id and execution_status=ACCEPTED|REJECTED|QUEUED.
- If action is accepted, the server guarantees it will include a final ACTION_RESULT fragment with tool_execution_id and deterministic result payload. If client reconnects, it will get ACTION_ACK and existing RESULT rather than cause duplication.

5) Partial-schema guidance for structured outputs
- To support merges and safe incremental parsing, server may emit a partial_schema_path (dot-path into a declared schema) that tells clients how to treat the fragment: append string, merge into object field, extend array, or replace subtree.
- Schema versioning: fragments reference a schema_id. If schema_id changes mid-response, server emits a SCHEMA_SWAP marker; clients should raise a non-fatal warning and continue best-effort reassembly.

6) Backpressure and small-client ergonomics
- Transport supports an explicit client->server window hint (max_frag_in_flight) to let SDKs throttle consumption/ACKs. This is advisory — server will respect for best-effort reduced memory on client devices.
- Mobile SDK default: max_frag_in_flight=4 and max_total_buffered_chars=64k. Desktop/servers default much higher.

7) SDK surface design (JS/Python proposals)
- StreamingResponse object: on('fragment', (frag)=>{}), on('action', (ack)=>{}), resume() (token), cancel(reason)
- Helper: ResponseBuilder that exposes applyFragment(frag) -> delta object and a toFinal() convenience. The builder hides partial json glue rules; app developers rarely call it directly.
- Action helper: createAction(spec) -> {fragment, idempotency_key}. The SDK auto-inserts a client-generated action_id and replays idempotency_key on resume.

8) Observability and billing signals
- Emit per-fragment telemetry: frag_seq, type, tokens_consumed (if measurable), latency_ms (server-to-frag), tool_exec_time_ms, error_code.
- Console surfaces a fragment timeline for a request (graph of frag_seq vs time) and a filter for ACTION_CALL fragments to inspect idempotency and execution states.

Implementation plan and incremental rollout
Phase 0 (experiment): server emits frag_seq and resume_token for a small percent of requests; SDKs ignore but capture for dev-mode testing.
Phase 1 (beta): clients can opt-in via header X-RI-Fragment=experimental; server streams fragments with deterministic headers. SDKs expose applyFragment and resume to early adopters.
Phase 2 (public): enable default for streaming endpoints with backwards-compat flags; Console shows fragment timelines and tool-call lifecycles.

Open questions / trade-offs
- resume_token size and privacy: token must not leak secret model state. Use HMAC'd opaque tokens. TTL? We should balance session length vs storage cost.
- Action id assignment: prefer client-generated IDs for early dedup but server-assigned ids help governance. Hybrid approach supported.
- Schema complexity: how prescriptive should partial_schema be? Keep it small (append, merge-field, extend-array, replace) to avoid heavy client schema libraries.
- Cost model: fragments increase telemetry granularity. Are we billing per fragment or per token? Prefer token billing with fragment-level telemetry for debugging.

Experiments and performance tests
- A/B test resume success rate for flaky mobile networks with and without fragments. Metric: percent of resumed sessions that produce identical final output.
- Measure server overhead: fragments per response distribution and cost delta for metadata headers.
- Latency tests: server should keep per-frag latency < configured SLO for first-frag and tail-frag.

Next steps and owners
- RFC write-up and proto sketch (Evan) — due 2025-03-07.
- SDK PoC (Maya) — JS + Python minimal streaming_response and ResponseBuilder by 2025-03-21.
- Server prototype (Ravi) — fragment headers, resume_token generation, ACTION_ACK/RESULT pipeline by 2025-03-21.
- Telemetry & Console mockups (Lina) — fragment timeline + per-frag logs by 2025-03-28.

Notes to reviewers
- Focus on client determinism and tool-call idempotency correctness first; schema-assisted merging is optional and should remain conservative.
- Consider small-client defaults strictly; we must not push heavy memory/CPU on mobile SDKs by default.
- Point reviewers to linked artifacts for a minimal wire-proto and an initial SDK sketch (PR 2345).

Working log (selected excerpts)
- 2025-02-20: prototype showed resume success increased from 72% -> 94% in a simulated 10% packet-drop environment.
- 2025-02-25: preliminary SDK builder simplified partial-json merging by using path-based inserts; still buggy for concurrent array edits.

This doc will be iterated after the RFC and first PoCs. Keep comments inline and mark unresolved items with [QUESTION].
